title: Large Construction
strapline: Crates, planks and tyres — big builds that need strong bodies and a team.
intent: Build whole-body strength and coordination through real lifting, hauling, pushing and balancing
Learn that some jobs are too big for one — recruiting help, negotiating a plan, holding your end steady
Make risk judgements for themselves: test the plank before you stand on it, check the crate before you climb
Think like engineers at body scale — ramps, bridges, towers and dens you can actually get inside
Use positional and comparative language where it really matters: heavier, longer, on top, underneath, next to
Turn a finished structure into a world — a bus, a boat, a castle — and keep the story going
implementation: Teach safe lifting and carrying explicitly — "two hands, bend your knees, ask a friend" — then trust children to do it
Stand back while children haul and struggle; the effort is the learning. Step in with a question, not a hand, first
Agree simple building-site rules WITH the children, and let them hold each other to them
Model testing before trusting: press the plank in the middle, wobble the crate, and say what you're checking for
Narrate the forces at work: "that plank's bending in the middle — is there a sturdier one?"
Once the build is finished, join the pretend on the children's terms — pay your bus fare, knock on the castle door
Leave good builds standing overnight where you can, so tomorrow starts with improving rather than restarting
key_questions: Do you think that plank will hold you? How could we test it first?
That crate looks too heavy for one person — who could help you?
How will you get the tyre all the way up to the top?
What does your build need next — a roof, a door, a ramp?
Which ramp is faster for the ball — the steep one or the long flat one? How do you know?

impact.text: Younger children push, pull, drag and carry big things on purpose — a tyre across the garden is a whole morning's work.
Children negotiate space and obstacles with control, stepping over planks and around each other's builds without collisions.
Children balance along planks and climb crate stacks with confidence and control — and know their own limits.
Children negotiate the build out loud — "you hold it steady, I'll push it up" — explaining their thinking and settling disagreements about the design.
Positional and comparative language turns up at body scale: which plank is longer, which crate is heavier, what goes on top and what underneath.
Children explore forces through play — ramps and rolling, balancing and bending, what tips and what holds.
Finished structures become buses, boats and castles, with shared storylines, assigned roles and negotiated props that run for days.
Children help agree the rules of the building site — helmets, two-hands carrying, no jumping from the top — and expect everyone to keep to them.

enhancements: A pulley and bucket rigged to the fence for hauling materials to the top of a build
Real (child-sized) hi-vis vests, clipboards and a laminated "site plan" board to draw the build first
Guttering and drainpipe lengths for water-and-ball run experiments off the finished structure
Large fabric, tarpaulins and pegs so any frame can become a den with a roof
A steering wheel, bell and bus-stop sign to tip a crate build into journey play
Log slices and rope alongside the crates for trickier, less regular building challenges

playing_exploring: Children take real, managed risks — climbing, balancing, testing — and learn what their bodies can do
The resources are big, open and unfinished, so every session starts with "what shall we build?"
active_learning: Big builds demand persistence — heavy things, high places and collapsing corners don't come right first time
Children feel the physical effort pay off: the plank finally sits flat, the tyre reaches the top
creating_thinking: Children plan out loud, test their predictions against gravity, and change strategy when the structure argues back
